abstract.para: Subvolumes divide a Btrfs file system into separate file and directory hierarchies. They are the units that you can mount, snapshot, include in or exclude from snapshots and delete independently.

section.title: What is a subvolume?
section.para: A Btrfs subvolume is a separately mountable file system within a physical partition. Each subvolume has its own independent file and directory hierarchy. Subvolumes appear as directories. You can manipulate them like any other directory, including renaming or moving them.

All subvolumes of a file system share the same pool of storage space. You do not need to define a size for a subvolume in advance. If required, you can limit the space of a subvolume with quota groups, as described in .

section.title: Top-level and default subvolumes
section.para: Every Btrfs file system contains a top-level subvolume with the ID 5. All other subvolumes are created below it. The default subvolume is the subvolume that the system mounts when you do not specify a subvolume explicitly. Initially, the top-level subvolume is the default subvolume.
You can change the default subvolume with the command btrfs subvolume set-default. Changing the default subvolume is the mechanism that allows booting from a snapshot after a rollback.

section.title: How to mount subvolumes?
section.para: You can mount each subvolume at a separate mount point. To select a subvolume, pass the subvol or subvolid mount option. Mounted subvolumes of the same file system share the underlying device.

section.title: Nested subvolumes
section.para: A subvolume can contain other subvolumes. A nested subvolume appears as a directory inside its parent subvolume. When you snapshot the parent, Btrfs does not include the content of nested subvolumes. In the snapshot, a nested subvolume appears as an empty directory.

This behavior is a deliberate design feature. Subvolumes allow you to include or exclude parts of a directory tree explicitly. For example, you can place frequently changing data such as logs or database files in a nested subvolume. A snapshot of the parent then stays small and a rollback of the parent does not overwrite that data.

section.title: Compression and copy-on-write properties
section.para: Btrfs supports transparent compression. When you enable it, Btrfs compresses file data when writing and decompresses it when reading. Enable it with the mount option compress or compress-force and select one of the algorithms zstd, lzo or zlib. Compression applies to new files only.

Subvolumes can contain files that change constantly, such as virtual machine images, database files or log files. For such data, copy-on-write can duplicate many blocks. To disable copy-on-write for a directory, set the C attribute on the empty directory. New files in this directory inherit the attribute:
Files with this attribute are not compressed and do not get checksums. After you create a snapshot, the first write to such a file still copies the shared blocks.
